title: Alexander
full_review:
In making movies, as in making war, "fortune favors the bold." Few film directors embody this ancient maxim more than Oliver Stone. Perhaps that is why he chose the proverb to open "Alexander" (Warner Bros.), his ambitious biopic about Alexander the Great. If nothing else, his three-hour sword-and-sandal spectacle is bold.

Exhibiting a creative hubris rivaling that of the world-conquering Macedonian, Stone has crafted an audacious film, dazzling viewers with epic battle scenes and eye-filling re-creations of splendiferous antiquity, while making sure that the movie's sweeping scope and din of charging chariots don't drown out the human drama at its heart.

The historic Alexander had, by age 25, mastered most of the known world, and, at his death in 323 B.C. at age 33, amassed an empire which stretched from Greece to India.

Echoing "Citizen Kane," the picture opens with Alexander (Colin Farrell) on his deathbed. The movie then leapfrogs ahead 40 years, where Ptolemy (Anthony Hopkins) -- one of Alexander's former generals and the film's narrator -- waxes poetic about his legendary liege ("I've known many great men in my life, but only one colossus"), distilling all that is to follow with the tragic truism: "All men reach and fall."

The sprawling narrative then backtracks to Alexander's youth, establishing the rancorous relationship between his conniving mother, Olympias (Angelina Jolie), who plants the seeds of Alexander's glory-greedy ambition by convincing him that he is a god, and his roughhewn, one-eyed father, King Philip (Val Kilmer), who warns him of the perils of Promethean pride. It also offers a brief snapshot of his early tutoring at the knee of the philosopher Aristotle (Christopher Plummer).

Alexander -- and the movie -- achieve larger-than-life status during the Battle of Guagamela, a spectacular and savage 12-minute clash between Alexander's vastly outnumbered troops and the army of his geopolitical archrival King Darius of Persia (Raz Degan). The gritty and graphic sequence is topped later by an even more intense jungle battle in India, involving rampaging war elephants. The latter contains the film's only concession to Stone's trademark psychedelic visual riffs.

But the movie is more than a catalog of Alexander's bloody conquests. Stone balances the grand-scale carnage of the battlefield with scenes of internecine power-mongering and racism among his generals, as well as the court intrigue and Oedipal dysfunction surrounding his ascension to the throne (told through flashbacks).

While not side-stepping the issue of Alexander's bisexuality, Stone exhibits restraint in addressing the Macedonian monarch's affections for childhood friend and lover Hephaistion (Jared Leto), discreetly conveying their intimate relationship through knowing, come-hither glances and manly hugs. The same cannot be said for either the several homoerotic scenes involving Alexander and an androgynous Persian eunuch, with whom he locks lips, or for the racy wedding night scene between Alexander and his feral Asiatic bride, Roxane (Rosario Dawson).

Though no actor can adequately fill Alexander's sandals, Farrell does an admirable job, imbuing the role with a blend of idealism, arrogance and relentless determination. And while he looks as silly in his ridiculous blonde wig as Richard Burton did when he played the Macedonian prince back in 1956, Farrell convincingly conveys Alexander's emotional arc from youthful bravado to war-weary sobriety, revealing a visionary driven as much by the Furies as by fate.

Though Christian viewers may find the film's brutalities and hedonism (not to mention Alexander's omnivorous sexual appetites) repelling, they must take into account the pre-Christian historical context of the world in which the events takes place.

"Alexander" has some epic flaws, including its interminable pacing, a disjointed script, one-dimensional characters, scene-chewing performances, risibly campy dialogue delivered in an odd assortment of accents (most of the Macedonians speak with lilting Irish brogues, while Jolie sounds Transylvanian) and an overly florid score by Vangelis.

Still, the movie also has its moments of impressive beauty, among them lavish scenes in Babylon which bring to life the opulence of the city's fabled Hanging Gardens. It also marks a more mature departure from the cinematic intemperance of such past Stone films as "Natural Born Killers" and "The Doors."

But in the end, like Alexander's 12-year campaign to unite East and West, the project proves too daunting. When many movies aspire to mediocrity, Stone deserves credit for the sheer chutzpah required for such a massive undertaking. And though his "Alexander" is far from great, what Ptolemy says about Alexander could just as easily apply to Stone, "His failures tower over other men's successes."

Due to strong battlefield violence and associated gore, an attempted rape, several implied gay sexual situations, one involving shadowy rear nudity, an explicit straight bedroom scene and generalized background debauchery, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
